classification.difficultyReason: Without intermediate prompts, select a nonparallel pair, derive its symbolic intersection, recognise the given expression in substitution into the third line, and establish the converse without assuming a nonzero pair determinant.

content.prompt:
Show that the three lines:
$$\begin{aligned}a_1x+b_1y+c_1&=0\\a_2x+b_2y+c_2&=0\\a_3x+b_3y+c_3&=0\end{aligned}$$
are concurrent, provided at least two of them are not parallel, if
$$\begin{aligned}&a_1(b_2c_3-b_3c_2)+a_2(b_3c_1-b_1c_3)\\&\qquad{}+a_3(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)=0.\end{aligned}$$
The converse is always true.

answer.short:
Writing $D=a_1b_2-a_2b_1$, a nonparallel first pair intersects at
$$\left(\frac{b_1c_2-b_2c_1}{D},\frac{a_2c_1-a_1c_2}{D}\right).$$
Substitution into the third equation gives zero precisely when the stated expression is zero. Conversely, substituting a common point into all three equations makes that expression zero.
answer.worked:
Relabel the lines if necessary so that the first two are not parallel. Put $D=a_1b_2-a_2b_1$, so $D\ne0$. Elimination gives
$$\begin{align*}Dx&=b_1c_2-b_2c_1\\x&=\frac{b_1c_2-b_2c_1}{D}\\Dy&=a_2c_1-a_1c_2\\y&=\frac{a_2c_1-a_1c_2}{D}.\end{align*}$$
Let
$$\begin{aligned}E&=a_1(b_2c_3-b_3c_2)+a_2(b_3c_1-b_1c_3)\\&\qquad{}+a_3(b_1c_2-b_2c_1).\end{aligned}$$
Expanding and collecting terms gives
$$E=a_3(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)+b_3(a_2c_1-a_1c_2)+c_3D.$$
At the intersection of the first two lines,
$$\begin{align*}a_3x+b_3y+c_3&=\frac{a_3(b_1c_2-b_2c_1)+b_3(a_2c_1-a_1c_2)+c_3D}{D}\\a_3x+b_3y+c_3&=\frac{E}{D}\\a_3x+b_3y+c_3&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus the intersection also lies on the third line, so the lines are concurrent.

Conversely, suppose $(h,k)$ lies on all three lines. Then $c_i=-a_ih-b_ik$ for $i=1,2,3$. Substitution gives
$$\begin{align*}b_1c_2-b_2c_1&=Dh\\a_2c_1-a_1c_2&=Dk\\E&=a_3Dh+b_3Dk+c_3D\\E&=D(a_3h+b_3k+c_3)\\E&=0.\end{align*}$$
This converse does not require $D\ne0$.
